title: Multiple Sclerosis: Why Time Matters
subtitle: Early recognition, diagnosis and treatment
audience: Neurologists, primary care physicians and nurses
disclaimer: Unbranded disease education for healthcare professionals. Not promotional and not medical advice. Treatment decisions should follow local guidelines and product labelling.

slides.title: MS at a glance
bullets: About 2.9 million people live with MS worldwide
Average age at diagnosis is 32
Women are affected about twice as often as men
A leading non-traumatic cause of disability in young adults
slides.speakerNotes: Multiple sclerosis is a chronic immune mediated disease of the central nervous system, in which the immune system attacks myelin and nerve fibres in the brain, spinal cord and optic nerves. Around two point nine million people live with it worldwide. It is usually diagnosed in early adulthood, at an average age of about thirty two, and women are affected roughly twice as often as men. Because it strikes people in their working and family building years, it is one of the leading causes of non traumatic disability in young adults.

slides.title: Recognising early MS
bullets: Optic neuritis: painful, blurred vision in one eye
Numbness, tingling or weakness in limbs or trunk
Double vision, vertigo or imbalance
Symptoms evolving over days and lasting more than 24 hours
slides.speakerNotes: The first event is often called a clinically isolated syndrome. Classic presentations include optic neuritis, with pain on eye movement and blurred vision in one eye, a partial spinal cord syndrome with numbness, tingling or a band like sensation around the trunk, or brainstem symptoms such as double vision and vertigo. These typically build over hours to days and last more than a day. Fatigue, bladder urgency and heat sensitivity are also common. Prompt referral to neurology for anyone with a suspected first demyelinating event is the single biggest step toward earlier diagnosis.

slides.title: Making the diagnosis
bullets: 2024 McDonald criteria: optic nerve added as a fifth region
Dissemination in time no longer always required
Supportive markers: central vein sign, kappa free light chains
Exclude mimics: misdiagnosis remains common
slides.speakerNotes: Diagnosis now follows the twenty twenty four revision of the McDonald criteria. MRI of the brain, spinal cord and optic nerves is central, and the optic nerve is now counted as a fifth typical region. Evidence of lesions at different points in time is no longer always required, so many people can be diagnosed at their first attack. Oligoclonal bands or kappa free light chains in the spinal fluid support the diagnosis, and the central vein sign and paramagnetic rim lesions on MRI help separate MS from its mimics. Excluding those mimics remains essential, because misdiagnosis still happens.

slides.title: The hidden progression
bullets: Damage continues between relapses, often silently
Most disability worsening occurs independent of relapses (PIRA)
Brain volume loss starts early in the disease
Relapse counts alone underestimate disease activity
slides.speakerNotes: One of the most important shifts in our understanding is that MS is active even when patients feel well. In large analyses of relapsing MS trials, most confirmed disability worsening happened without any preceding relapse. Neurologists call this progression independent of relapse activity. Brain volume loss and silent new MRI lesions can accumulate from the earliest stages. The practical message is that counting relapses alone underestimates disease activity, and that structured monitoring, including regular MRI and careful assessment of subtle changes in walking, hand function and cognition, is essential.

slides.title: Why early treatment matters
bullets: Disease-modifying therapies reduce relapses and new lesions
Injectable, oral and high-efficacy monoclonal antibody options
Earlier high-efficacy therapy linked to less long-term disability
Shared decisions balance efficacy, safety and life plans
slides.speakerNotes: Because damage begins early, the window for protecting the brain is early too. Disease modifying therapies reduce relapses and new MRI lesions, and the options now range from injectable therapies, to oral medicines, to high efficacy monoclonal antibodies. Observational data from large registries suggest that starting a high efficacy therapy within the first two years is associated with less disability years later, compared with starting it later in the disease. The right choice is always individual, weighing efficacy, safety, monitoring needs, comorbidities and plans such as pregnancy.

slides.title: Monitoring and partnership
bullets: Baseline and at least annual MRI on treatment
Check infections and update vaccines before starting treatment
Address smoking, vitamin D, exercise and mental health
Multidisciplinary care and patient support improve adherence
slides.speakerNotes: Good outcomes depend on what happens after the first prescription. A fresh baseline MRI after starting treatment and at least annual scans help detect silent activity and guide decisions about switching therapy. Before immune therapies, screening for infections such as hepatitis B and updating vaccinations are important. Lifestyle matters too. Stopping smoking, staying active, optimising vitamin D and supporting mental health all contribute. Finally, a multidisciplinary team, including specialist nurses, rehabilitation and patient support programmes, helps people stay on treatment. I am happy to share the underlying publications on any of these points.
